title: Predictive electronic feedback control for narrow-linewidth lasers
authors: Jiatian Liu, Xuan Qi, Xiayang Fan, Shenchao Jin, Yuan Sun
abstract: Narrow-linewidth lasers are essential for various key atom-laser interaction processes and optical setups in quantum coherent control, quantum precision measurement, and quantum information science. The Pound-Drever-Hall (PDH) technique is the standard method for the frequency-stabilization of narrow-linewidth lasers, but the inherent time delay in its feedback loop inevitably induces excessive phase noise, commonly known as servo bumps. Previous solutions primarily rely on additional optical components outside the electronic feedback control loop. Here, we propose and implement a generic method based on the Smith predictor to address the time-delay issue entirely within the electronic part of the PDH feedback control loop. We systematically demonstrate its capability to suppress phase noise and reduce servo bumps by adding only a single Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) controller to the loop. This class of methods is demonstrated to be conceptually concise with minimal hardware overhead, effective in practice, and holds potential for a wide variety of future applications.
summary: This paper introduces a novel electronic control method using the Smith predictor to overcome phase noise ('servo bumps') caused by time delays in PDH laser stabilization. By implementing the predictor on an FPGA, the authors compensate for loop delays entirely in the electronics, significantly improving the stability and signal-to-noise ratio for quantum applications like atomic clocks and quantum sensing.
main_problem: The standard Pound-Drever-Hall (PDH) technique for stabilizing narrow-linewidth lasers suffers from excessive phase noise, known as 'servo bumps,' due to inherent time delays in the electronic feedback loop.
main_result: The proposed method successfully suppresses these servo bumps by compensating for the time delay entirely within the electronic feedback path, achieving significant noise reduction (e.g., 14 dB suppression) without adding extra optical components.
method: The authors implement a Smith predictor, a classical control theory tool, digitally on an FPGA to model and compensate for the total time delay in the PDH feedback loop.
model_or_system: The system involves stabilizing a narrow-linewidth laser frequency using the PDH technique, which is crucial for quantum coherent control and quantum information science. The core challenge is the time delay ($	au$) in the feedback loop.
key_observables: Phase noise spectra, servo bump magnitude (dB), locked-state error signal attenuation, and correlation coefficient in quantum sensing.
important_parameters: Time delays ($	au_1, 	au_2$), feedback bandwidth, and the residual error bound (e.g., 20 kHz cutoff).
main_assumptions: The method assumes the system's delay properties remain invariant over time, and residual error is bounded by a high-pass filter.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the theoretical block diagram of the Smith predictor integration, the experimental setup, and spectral comparisons showing the suppression of noise bumps with and without the predictor.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of delay-induced noise in PDH locking, proposes the Smith predictor implementation on an FPGA, details the compensation mechanism, and validates the method through frequency response characterization and quantum sensing experiments.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, hardware-efficient control technique applicable to any delay-limited quantum optical measurement, directly improving the signal-to-noise ratio for quantum sensing applications.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Basic design, experimental setup and control system architecture. (a) Theoretical block diagram of the closed-loop control system incorporating a Smith predictor, illustrating the inherent system time delays (τ1 and τ2) and the mathematical signal flow for delay compensation. U(s) is the Laplace transform of the control signal U(t) defined on the time domain [0, ∞) for a prescribed starting time t = 0. (b) Schematic of the experimental setup, demonstrating the integration of the Smith predictor for evaluating and suppressing system phase noise. HWP, Half-Wave Plate. QWP, Quarter-Wave Plate. PBS, Polarizing Beamsplitter. EOM, Electro-Optic Modulator. AOM, Acousto-Optic Modulator....

FIG. 2: Top: Open-loop magnitude response of the plant, |G(jω)|. The blue line represents the plant gain (dB) extracted from the closed-loop system, illustrating its inherent frequency attenuation characteristics. Bottom: Open-loop phase response of the plant, ∠G(jω). The red line denotes the unwrapped phase (deg), clearly demonstrating the linear phase lag induced by hardware time delay.

FIG. 3: Spectral analysis of the PDH locking system without (red traces) and with (blue traces) the proposed method using Smith predictor. (a) Beat-note signal spectrum centered at the 80 MHz carrier frequency. (b) Error signal spectrum in the locked state.

FIG. 4: Experimental performance versus key parameters. The left vertical axis denotes the servo-bump level and the right vertical axis its peak frequency. Filled and open markers correspond to the left and right vertical axes, respectively; stars denote the original peak positions.

FIG. 5: Experimental results of the Rydberg atom quantum sensing. The red and blue traces correspond to the system operating without and with the proposed method of predictive electronic feedback control, respectively. (a) Spectra of error signals of the probe beam in the locked state. (b) Spectra of the transmission signal of probe laser via Rydberg EIT.
